summary: This program creates three Room objects using the class's no-argument constructor and prints each one, so you can see the default values a new object starts with.

lines.text: A separate class holds the program's starting point, keeping the driver code apart from the Room domain class that describes a single room.
This is the method the Java launcher calls first, so everything the program does begins here.
The `new` keyword asks Java for a fresh Room in memory, and the empty parentheses select the constructor that takes no arguments; the variable `room1` then refers to that object.
Each `new` produces a completely separate object, so room2 has its own copy of the fields even though it was built from the same blueprint.
A third object proves the point: one class can be used to create as many instances as the program needs.
A short label makes the output easier to read once the three room descriptions follow.
Passing an object to println quietly calls its toString method, which is why you see a readable description of the room instead of a memory address.
